meta.title: Fleet Watch — maritime chokepoints
meta.note: Six chokepoints chosen for direct EU trade relevance. Summaries are grounded in real, current reporting (retrieved via web research) — not decorative. Update as events develop; each item carries its own source.

items.name: Strait of Gibraltar
items.summary: Over 300 vessels cross the 14km strait every day — roughly one every five minutes. Port congestion at Algeciras and Tanger Med causes recurring delays, and the strait is one of Europe's primary irregular-migration routes from Africa, with Morocco's control of departures giving it real leverage over Spain and the EU.
items.sourceLabel: The World Data — Strait of Gibraltar Statistics

items.name: Dover Strait / English Channel
items.summary: The world's busiest shipping lane by vessel count — over 400 transits a day through a strait just 33km wide, demanding constant traffic management. The same narrow water carries a humanitarian crisis: around 41,000 people crossed by small boat in 2025, and a UK–France returns pilot has so far had limited effect.
items.sourceLabel: Ballast Markets — Dover Strait chokepoint brief

items.name: Danish Straits
items.summary: An estimated 90 Russian "shadow fleet" tankers a month transit the Great Belt and Øresund carrying sanctioned oil — often uninsured, flag-hopping, and running with AIS transponders switched off. Nordic-Baltic states are now demanding proof of insurance before transit, but the spill risk from aging, uncovered vessels remains high.
items.sourceLabel: Ballast Markets — Danish Straits shadow-fleet brief

items.name: Bosphorus / Turkish Straits
items.summary: Governed since 1936 by the Montreux Convention — marking 90 years in 2026 — the Bosphorus is a vital grain and energy corridor into and out of the Black Sea, and chronically congested. Turkey's proposed Istanbul Canal is pitched as a fix, but critics argue its real purpose is to let Ankara sidestep Montreux's traffic rules entirely.

items.name: Suez Canal
items.summary: Traffic remains roughly 60% below pre-crisis levels in early 2026, two years into Red Sea diversions around the Cape of Good Hope. Egypt's estimated revenue loss is near $10bn, though 2026 forecasts point to a gradual recovery as security conditions in the Red Sea slowly improve.

items.name: Bab-el-Mandeb / Red Sea
items.summary: Around 8% of the world's seaborne oil passes this strait, and Houthi attacks and blockade threats against shipping continued into mid-2026, repeatedly pushing traffic to divert north into the Suez approach or turn back entirely — the direct cause of the Suez Canal's own extended slump.
items.sourceLabel: The Hill — Red Sea shipping slows after Houthi attacks
